Japanese stimulus selection: frequency, familiarity, AoA and BOI

Source: vignettes/japanese-stimuli.Rmd
japanese-stimuli.Rmd

For a Japanese word-recognition experiment, you may want to vary BOI while inspecting frequency, familiarity and acquisition ratings as other item characteristics. This guide joins those sources by study item ID, retains unresolved and unmatched items, and shows distributions and missingness within each condition. It provides a review table, not automatic stimulus matching or evidence that conditions are balanced. The small item set below illustrates data handling; it is not a recommended experimental design.

The code uses existing lexdiv_norm_profile() calculations and three installed example scripts. These scripts are explicitly sourced helpers, not exported package functions. All operations after file acquisition run in R, without Python. Source tables and derived norm values are obtained separately; no external values are embedded in this guide. Each real-data chunk below requires the specified local files and is not executed during package installation.

Fix the frequency table and lexical unit

Use TUBELEX (Nohejl et al., 2025), Japanese tubelex-ja-base-pos.tsv.xz, at commit 7cb5fb36add76b83a266d1967536e1a1d3faa513. This is the orthographic base (orthBase) table using unidic-lite 1.0.8 (UniDic 2.1.2), not the surface, lemma or UniDic 3.1.0 table. The helper checks the exact compressed-file SHA-256: be1a66ac600d5e7efe6a301f63fba5321352742ae5dbaaa231529cdf2ab11710.

The upstream format provides counts and the number of videos/channels containing each key. The final [TOTAL] row supplies denominators: 165,932,178 tokens, 100,660 videos and 30,550 channels. Counts include special tokens such as <num>; the denominator is not recomputed after selecting study items or POS. The helper returns count / total_count * 1e6, videos / total_videos and channels / total_channels, without smoothing. These last two are proportions, unlike the log scores of the bundled English tubelex_profile().

Acquire the frequency file explicitly, once:

data_dir <- "japanese-resources"
dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
revision <- "7cb5fb36add76b83a266d1967536e1a1d3faa513"
frequency_path <- file.path(data_dir, "tubelex-ja-base-pos.tsv.xz")
if (!file.exists(frequency_path)) {
  download.file(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/naist-nlp/tubelex/",
    revision, "/frequencies/tubelex-ja-base-pos.tsv.xz"),
    frequency_path, mode = "wb")
}

Retain the upstream BSD-3-Clause notice and cite the paper when using TUBELEX. Aggregate-frequency availability does not make the original subtitles a redistributable corpus. For the other sources, follow the Japanese norms guide: WLSP-familiarity v4.0 is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; the inspected AoA data are CC BY-NC 4.0; the BOI OSF project specifies CC BY 4.0. The package code license does not replace those terms for your joined table.

Review the keys before joining

Keep term as the norm lookup spelling and orth_base as the reviewed frequency key. For example, 食べた can use frequency base 食べる, while AoA/BOI lookup still uses 食べた; substituting a base-form rating would be a separate decision. 人気 in two contexts receives the same base-key frequency. The TUBELEX pos column is the majority POS for a key, not a disambiguated frequency. Neither a reading nor a WLSP record selection splits that aggregate count.

items <- data.frame(
  item_id = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5"),
  condition = c(rep("A", 4), rep("B", 5)),
  term = c("学校", "犬", "人気", "食べた", "猫", "椅子", "人気", "未登録の例語", "青い空"),
  context = c("school", "animal", "popularity", "ate", "animal", "chair",
              "presence of people", "unmatched illustration", "multiword phrase"),
  orth_base = c("学校", "犬", "人気", "食べる", "猫", "椅子", "人気", "未登録の例語", NA_character_),
  base_reason = c(rep("Manually reviewed base for this illustration", 7),
    "Deliberately absent test key, not an observed lexical base",
    "Multiple words; no single orthBase assigned")
)
source(system.file("examples", "japanese-tubelex.R", package = "ldfreq"))
frequency <- profile_japanese_tubelex_items(items, frequency_path)
frequency$items[, c("item_id", "term", "orth_base", "tubelex_lookup_term",
                    "tubelex_status", "tubelex_per_million")]

The helper performs NFKC then lowercase after you supply the base. It keeps the original forms and a normalization-change flag. It does not trim strings, guess a base, tokenize phrases, or replace an unmatched key with a lemma. A missing base is unresolved_base, an absent supplied key is unmatched, and both retain NA counts, not zero. Its generic profile contains only queried items; profile_item_ids maps those rows back to the full item table. Use the full table as the denominator for stimulus selection.

For corpus tokens, use the optional gibasa/UniDic recipe in Japanese annotations. After inspecting selected from that guide, its original positions and orthBase can be connected as follows:

token_items <- data.frame(item_id = paste0("token-", seq_len(nrow(selected))),
  document_id = selected$document_id, segment_id = selected$segment_id,
  token_index = selected$token_index, term = selected$surface,
  orth_base = selected$orthBase,
  base_reason = "gibasa 1.1.3; UniDic 2.1.2 / unidic-lite 1.0.8; reviewed selection")
token_frequency <- profile_japanese_tubelex_items(token_items, frequency_path)
saveRDS(list(imported = ja, selection = selection, frequency = token_frequency),
        "japanese-token-frequency.rds")

This is a reviewed base-key lookup, not a reproduction of the full TUBELEX tokenizer. Upstream converts fullwidth tilde before tokenization, handles numbers/placeholders and uses surface fallback for unknown nodes; the gibasa recipe does not reproduce all those steps or expose a verified unknown-node flag. Do not normalize raw text before annotation merely to increase coverage: that can alter segmentation and source positions. Record any separate text transformation, dictionary hashes and excluded tokens. The saved imported object retains those declarations and positions. This lookup does not establish accuracy on learner errors or equivalence between English and Japanese measures.

Combine ratings while keeping decisions and missingness

Place the separately acquired, pinned files documented in the norms guide in data_dir. Review all WLSP candidates before recording your choices; even a unique candidate requires an explicit decision. The selections below illustrate those decisions for the stated contexts, not validated sense-specific norms.

source(system.file("examples", "japanese-norms.R", package = "ldfreq"))
source(system.file("examples", "wlsp-items.R", package = "ldfreq"))
aoa <- profile_japanese_norm_items(items, file.path(data_dir, "data_AoA.csv"), "aoa")
boi <- profile_japanese_norm_items(items, file.path(data_dir, "data_boi.csv"), "boi")
wlsp_path <- file.path(data_dir, "bunruidb-fam.csv")
review <- review_wlsp_items(items, wlsp_path)
review$candidates
decisions <- data.frame(item_id = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2", "b3"),
  record_id = c("022471", "062994", "033333", "063080", "053482", "002375"),
  reason = c("School context", "Animal, not occupational metaphor", "Popularity reading ninki",
             "Animal context", "Furniture context", "Presence reading hitoke"))
wlsp <- review_wlsp_items(items, wlsp_path, decisions)

# Each item appears once. Never merge by spelling: 人気 has two study IDs.
joined <- frequency$items
for (name in c("aoa", "boi", "wlsp")) {
  result <- list(aoa = aoa, boi = boi, wlsp = wlsp)[[name]]$items
  index <- match(joined$item_id, result$item_id)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(result$item_id), !anyNA(index), nrow(result) == nrow(items))
  fields <- setdiff(names(result), names(items))
  added <- result[index, fields, drop = FALSE]
  if (name != "wlsp") names(added) <- sub("^norm_", paste0(name, "_"), fields)
  stopifnot(!any(names(added) %in% names(joined)))
  joined[names(added)] <- added
}
stopifnot(identical(joined$item_id, items$item_id))
joined[, c("item_id", "condition", "tubelex_status", "wlsp_status",
           "aoa_lookup_status", "boi_lookup_status")]

AoA is a mean of seven rating categories, not years; category 7 includes both 12+ years and unknown age. BOI is a separate seven-point rating. WLSP know is a published Bayesian estimate, not an NTT seven-point rating. Adult native-speaker norms do not measure an individual learner’s knowledge or ability to employ a word appropriately. The BOI publication/correction scope and WLSP estimation caveats remain as documented in the norms guide and helper metadata.

Inspect every condition and each available subset 

measure_columns <- c(frequency = "tubelex_per_million", familiarity = "wlsp_know",
                     aoa = "aoa_mean", boi = "boi_mean")
coverage <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(joined, joined$condition), function(x) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(measure_columns), function(measure) {
    value <- x[[measure_columns[[measure]]]]
    observed <- value[!is.na(value)]
    q <- if (length(observed)) unname(quantile(observed, c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1))) else rep(NA_real_, 5)
    data.frame(condition = x$condition[1], measure, total = nrow(x),
      observed = length(observed), missing = sum(is.na(value)),
      mean = if (length(observed)) mean(observed) else NA_real_,
      sd = if (length(observed) > 1) sd(observed) else NA_real_,
      min = q[1], q25 = q[2], median = q[3], q75 = q[4], max = q[5])
  }))
}))
rownames(coverage) <- NULL
coverage
complete <- complete.cases(joined[unname(measure_columns)])
table(condition = joined$condition, all_four_observed = complete)
joined[!complete, c("item_id", "condition", "tubelex_status", "wlsp_status",
                    "aoa_lookup_status", "boi_lookup_status")]

# Show the individual observations, not just condition means.
pdf("japanese-stimulus-distributions.pdf", width = 8, height = 7)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (measure in names(measure_columns)) {
  value <- joined[[measure_columns[[measure]]]]
  if (measure == "frequency") value <- log10(value) # matched positive counts only
  if (any(is.finite(value))) {
    stripchart(value ~ joined$condition, vertical = TRUE, method = "stack", pch = 16,
      xlab = "Condition", ylab = if (measure == "frequency") "log10(per million)" else measure)
  } else { plot.new(); message(measure, " has no observed values; see the coverage table.") }
}
dev.off()

Select potential confounds based on the research question, not on which columns make condition means look similar. Decide in advance how to handle missing items, acceptable imbalance and correlations among predictors. Equal means or non-significant tests do not establish balance. Check the complete subset separately: excluding unmatched items can change the lexical population. Record any replacements and repeat the inspection on the final item IDs. Do not sum these measures into a composite difficulty score.

bundle <- list(items = joined, coverage = coverage, complete = complete,
  frequency = frequency, aoa = aoa, boi = boi, wlsp = wlsp, session = sessionInfo())
saveRDS(bundle, "japanese-stimulus-review.rds")
write.csv(joined, "japanese-stimulus-review.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
restored <- readRDS("japanese-stimulus-review.rds")
stopifnot(identical(restored$items, joined), identical(restored$wlsp$decisions, decisions))

RDS preserves source hashes, denominators, mapping decisions and the complete profile objects; CSV is a convenient review table but lacks that provenance. Keep the acquired files in a permitted local archive. Sharing joined values requires respecting each source’s terms. To report the analysis, specify the study population and task, lexical unit, resource versions, selected WLSP estimate, base-form choices, per-condition missingness and retained item IDs.
